passages.text: One DSD People, Access and Culture | 1 Facilitator Guide One DSD People, Access and Culture Use this guide with the three adapted training companions and their corresponding courses in the full application. It supports thoughtful discussion, clear explanations, and voluntary practice for staff and supervisors. For all staff, including supervisors and managers. Participation is voluntary. You may use the practice cases, reflect privately, discuss an example, or pass. No one needs to disclose personal experiences, identities, or assessment results. Participation and course completion in this program do not count toward DHS-required training credits unless management, a director, or DHS leadership expressly approves an exception.

passages.label: page 2
passages.text: One DSD People, Access and Culture | 2 Use the courses together or separately These companions support the full application's courses on white privilege, unconscious bias, and intercultural competence. Choose the subject that fits the group's question. Read the explanation before using the case, then allow people to compare responses and examine the feedback. No fixed session length or compulsory sequence is part of this guide. The One DSD Team and consultant can review these materials together when choosing Learning Lab topics and resources for further development. Learning Labs already take place every other meeting. The Team decides what to explore and who facilitates. Decisions about developing a full Articulate 360 course for DHS Pathlore remain a shared selection process; these materials do not represent a completed Pathlore course. Prepare for participation Read the selected lesson and its sources. Have the practice case and answer explanation available in a readable format. Offer spoken or written participation, time to consider a question, and the option to pass. Describe any visual information needed for an activity rather than relying on an image alone. Use the glossary to explain an unfamiliar term briefly, then return to the question. Check the actual accessibility and communication arrangements for the meeting. Do not ask someone to disclose a disability or personal history in order to choose a learning format.

passages.label: page 3
passages.text: One DSD People, Access and Culture | 3 Open with clear choices A suggested opening is: 'We are here to examine how everyday decisions and communication affect people. We will use practice examples. You are welcome to ask questions, write privately, join the discussion, or pass. No one is expected to speak for a community or share a personal experience.' Invite respectful disagreement with ideas and attention to evidence. Do not promise absolute confidentiality in a workplace discussion. Ask participants to avoid identifiable details about colleagues, community members, or service recipients. Explain any actual meeting recording or sharing arrangements before the activity; this guide does not authorize recording. Facilitate white privilege learning Begin with the distinction between effort and an additional barrier a person may or may not face. Use the college example to examine that distinction without ranking hardship. Then use the opportunity example to move from individual experience to a process the group can examine. If someone asks a colleague of color to provide proof through a personal story, remove that expectation and return to the practice case. Keep the learning open to all staff. Do not assign attendance or participation by racial identity, use a public privilege score, or require a personal disclosure activity. If someone questions the term, ask which part is unclear and explain the particular advantage or barrier under discussion. Questions are an opportunity to clarify the reasoning. Neither disagreement nor discomfort is evidence of a person's character or intercultural stage.

passages.label: page 4
passages.text: One DSD People, Access and Culture | 4 Facilitate unconscious bias learning Ask participants to separate what they can observe from what they have inferred. Use the phone example instead of asking people to judge strangers from photographs. Discuss more than one plausible explanation, then identify information that could distinguish them. In the proposal example, compare evidence against the same relevant criteria. When discussing affinity, confirmation, halo, and perception effects, examine the reasoning rather than diagnosing the person. An affinity group or a relationship is not itself proof of an unfair decision. Use the complaint example to show how an unsupported label can become a repeated practice. Do not debate the merits of an actual complaint during the learning session. No IAT result is required, collected, or used to evaluate an employee. Older national occupational statistics are not evidence of the current DSD workforce. Facilitate intercultural learning Connect each example to a question about meaning. A document put aside, a pause, or a concern about a service can have several explanations. Ask what the person has said and what remains unknown before proposing an adjustment. Use the five IDC orientations as concepts for understanding ways of approaching difference. Do not invite participants to estimate their own placement, move themselves down an imagined scale, or identify a colleague's orientation. Personal assessment and feedback are separate from these learning activities. When the group discusses adaptation, ask what changed because a perspective was understood more fully. A helpful action by itself does not prove assessed developmental movement. Culture should inform inquiry without becoming an all-purpose explanation for language access, disability, organizational expectations, or an individual's preference.

passages.label: page 5
passages.text: One DSD People, Access and Culture | 5 Respond when a discussion becomes difficult Pause a personal label or stereotype and bring the discussion back to the specific words, decision, or practice. You might say: 'Let's separate the action we can describe from the motive we are assigning.' If a participant identifies harm, acknowledge the concern and offer a choice about continuing; do not require public reconciliation or reassurance. When a real personnel, discrimination, service, or safety concern arises, explain that the learning discussion cannot decide it. Support use of the relevant agency process without asking the group to investigate. Native American and Tribal-specific questions should be referred to the appropriate DHS or ADSA office responsible for Tribal matters; this guide does not supply that specialized instruction. Close with a useful reflection Invite each person to identify one question they understand differently or one practice they may want to examine. Sharing is optional. Someone may choose a personal reflection, a practice example, or an issue within their responsibilities. Do not create reporting duties, deadlines, or assignments that the group has not agreed to. Ask for feedback on clarity, relevance, and accessibility. Treat a correct activity response as evidence of that response, not a diagnosis or a guarantee of future conduct. Connect further questions to the existing courses, Equity Analysis Toolkit, or an appropriate source of guidance. passages.label: page 1
passages.text: One DSD People, Access and Culture | 1 Intercultural Competence in Practice One DSD People, Access and Culture Foundation learning for all staff and supervisors Intercultural learning helps us examine our own assumptions, understand how another person makes meaning, and adjust our response thoughtfully. These activities connect that learning to communication, team decisions, policies, and services across the division. Cultural knowledge can prepare a useful question; the person and situation still matter. For all staff, including supervisors and managers. Participation is voluntary. You may use the practice cases, reflect privately, discuss an example, or pass. No one needs to disclose personal experiences, identities, or assessment results. What you will practice Connect a good intention with a useful response Ask about meaning without surrendering judgment Use cultural knowledge as a starting point Check understanding when a resource is not used Practice perspective taking and adaptation Use feedback to keep learning Use with the full course https://one-dsd-people-access-culture-production.up.railway.app/courses/dc-i7-what-intercultural-competence- means Participation and course completion in this program do not count toward DHS-required training credits unless management, a director, or DHS leadership expressly approves an exception.

passages.label: page 2
passages.text: One DSD People, Access and Culture | 2 1 Connect a good intention with a useful response A helpful intention does not tell us whether a response fits another person's needs. We may offer the kind of explanation or support that works for us and assume it works for everyone. Intercultural practice asks us to examine that expectation and learn what the other person means. In a work setting, adapting a response includes clarity about what can change. You can explain information differently, ask about communication preferences, or make a discussion easier to join while keeping relevant requirements clear. Understanding a perspective does not require agreeing with every request. Explore the example Practice example: A team sends a detailed written summary because the writer finds long explanations reassuring. Several readers say they cannot locate the action they need to take. The writer's intention was helpful; the format still needs attention. Try it Identify the writer's assumption. Draft a short opening that explains the action and offers access to detail. Ask what response format would be useful without assuming that a reader's identity explains their preference. Compare the revised response with the original purpose. Check your reasoning Which response best connects intention with the reader's experience? A. Keep the message unchanged because the writer meant well. B. Assume all readers want less information. C. Ask what readers need to act and revise the format while preserving necessary detail. Answer C. The third response checks whether the communication works for its audience while keeping the important information available. Reflect if useful: What do I tend to offer because it helps me, before asking whether it helps someone else?

passages.label: page 3
passages.text: One DSD People, Access and Culture | 3 2 Ask about meaning without surrendering judgment Curiosity works best when it has a relevant purpose. You do not need a person's family history or cultural identity to ask what a word means to them in the current conversation. Explain why you are asking, listen to the response, and avoid pressing for personal information that the task does not require. Openness also includes examining your own interpretation. A person may use a familiar word differently or associate a service with an earlier experience. You can acknowledge that meaning and explain the actual program without promising eligibility, changing a requirement, or dismissing the concern. Explore the example Practice example: A person declines information about a service because they call it 'welfare' and do not want to apply. The staff member does not assume this reflects the beliefs of all people in the person's town, age group, or community. They ask what concerns the person has and explain the service accurately. Try it Write a respectful question about the concern. Then write a clear explanation using only information you would need to verify about the actual service. Leave the choice with the person. In this practice activity, do not invent eligibility rules or a guaranteed benefit. Check your reasoning What should guide the staff member's response? A. The person's stated concern and accurate information about the service. B. A general assumption about rural communities. C. A promise that applying will produce the preferred result. Answer A. The first response attends to this person and the actual service. A group stereotype or an unverified promise would not establish understanding. Reflect if useful: How could I ask a useful question without making someone feel they must explain an entire culture?

passages.label: page 4
passages.text: One DSD People, Access and Culture | 4 3 Use cultural knowledge as a starting point People draw on many experiences, including family, profession, language, community, and organizational habits. A reference about a cultural pattern may help you recognize a possibility. It cannot tell you why a particular person acted or what they need. Treat it as preparation for listening, not as a personal profile. The same care applies to your own familiar practices. What a team calls normal may depend on experience that newcomers do not share. Explaining those expectations can reduce the need to guess and make disagreement easier to express. Explore the example Practice example: A colleague pauses when asked to disagree with a proposal in a large meeting. Someone attributes the pause to the colleague's nationality. Later, the colleague says they needed to read an attachment before responding. The group description did not explain this exchange. Try it List the observation, the initial interpretation, and two other explanations. Draft a question about what the colleague needs to respond. Identify one team habit that could be made clearer for everyone, such as sharing the material before asking for a decision. Check your reasoning How should a cultural reference be used here? A. As proof of the colleague's reason for pausing. B. As background that may inform a question, while checking the actual situation. C. As a reason to stop asking the colleague for input. Answer B. The second response allows context to inform inquiry without substituting a group description for the person's own account. Reflect if useful: Which unwritten expectations have become invisible to me because I know the setting well?

passages.label: page 5
passages.text: One DSD People, Access and Culture | 5 4 Check understanding when a resource is not used Providing a resource does not establish that it is understandable or useful. A translated document, for example, may still contain unfamiliar terms or fail to answer the person's question. Putting it aside does not establish a literacy level, a cultural belief, or a lack of interest. Ask about the task and the person's preferred way to discuss it. When communication support is needed, use the appropriate agency arrangements. A learning example should not encourage a staff member to improvise interpretation or make promises about a service they cannot authorize. Explore the example Practice example: A staff member offers a translated notice about a renewal process. The person puts it aside and says they have no questions. The staff member asks whether it would help to go through the next step together and what form of explanation would be useful. Try it Draft a follow-up that invites a choice rather than testing the person. State what you still do not know. Explain how you would check the actual communication arrangements for the service instead of guessing what assistance is available. Check your reasoning What does putting the notice aside establish? A. That the person cannot read it. B. That the person's culture rejects written information. C. Only that the notice was put aside; its meaning still needs to be checked. Answer C. The third answer stays with the observation. A respectful question is needed before drawing conclusions about understanding or preference. Reflect if useful: How can I check whether my explanation helped without making the other person feel tested?

passages.label: page 6
passages.text: One DSD People, Access and Culture | 6 5 Practice perspective taking and adaptation The Intercultural Development Continuum describes five orientations: Denial overlooks cultural difference; Polarization judges it through an us-and-them view; Minimization emphasizes shared experience in ways that may hide difference; Acceptance seeks deeper understanding; Adaptation brings that understanding into a response. This is a brief introduction to the model, not a method for scoring yourself or another person. You can examine the reasoning in a practice response without assigning an orientation to its speaker. In practice, ask what a different perspective changes about your options. An adjustment should respond to the situation and remain open to feedback. Explore the example Practice example: A planning group says everyone values independence, so one approach should work for all. A participant explains that, for them, choosing support from trusted people is part of independence. The group asks how its options could respect that meaning while preserving the person's own choice. Try it Identify what the shared word concealed. Draft an option that responds to the explanation rather than treating the group as culturally uniform. Explain why this is an example to discuss, not enough information to assign anyone an IDI result. Check your reasoning What can you reasonably conclude from the example? A. A stated perspective gives the group a reason to reconsider its options. B. The participant has reached a specific IDI score. C. Everyone in the participant's community defines independence the same way. Answer A. The first conclusion follows from the example. One exchange cannot establish an assessment result or a rule about an entire community. Reflect if useful: What familiar value could carry a different practical meaning for someone else?

passages.label: page 7
passages.text: One DSD People, Access and Culture | 7 6 Use feedback to keep learning A useful reflection names an assumption, an adjustment, and what you learned about its effect. You can explore your own habits privately or examine a practice example with colleagues. Neither route requires a personal assessment result. If you have an IDI development plan, you may choose learning that fits your own goals without sharing that plan. Feedback is most useful when it describes an exchange clearly: what was said, what was understood, and what would make the next conversation more useful. Avoid turning one helpful action into a claim that a person has reached a developmental stage or mastered intercultural practice. Explore the example Practice example: A team shares questions before a discussion and offers a written response option. A participant says the advance questions helped them prepare, but an unexplained term still prevented a clear response. The team keeps the useful change and revises the term. Try it Write a short learning note about the practice case. Name what helped, what remained unclear, and what the team could try next. Connect the question to the application's intercultural continuum or cultural humility course if further learning would be useful. Check your reasoning Which feedback best supports continued practice? A. You are now fully interculturally competent. B. The advance questions helped preparation; explaining the unfamiliar term would make the next exchange clearer. C. Anyone who still needs an explanation is at a lower stage. Answer B. The second response is specific and usable. It describes the exchange without ranking people or claiming a completed developmental journey. Reflect if useful: What would I like to understand more fully about my own assumptions or another perspective?

passages.label: page 1
passages.text: One DSD People, Access and Culture | 1 Learning Glossary Use these explanations to support discussion across the full One DSD application. They are learning definitions, not substitutes for legal definitions or agency policy. Race A social classification shaped by history and social practices, often associated with perceived physical differences. Racial categories can affect treatment and opportunity; they do not establish a person's ability, character, or culture. Ethnicity A connection with shared cultural heritage, ancestry, language, traditions, or history. A person may describe several connections. Race and ethnicity are related in some settings but are not interchangeable. Culture Learned and changing ways people make meaning and organize life. Family, community, work, and other settings contribute. A group description does not predict every member's beliefs or behavior. Stereotype A generalized belief about a group that is applied to a person without sufficient attention to their circumstances. A seemingly favorable stereotype can also create unfair expectations. Prejudice A judgment or attitude about people based on their perceived group membership rather than a fair consideration of the person or situation. Discrimination Unequal treatment or exclusion related to a characteristic such as race or disability. In this learning material, the term invites examination of conduct and effects. Formal findings depend on applicable requirements and the appropriate review process.

passages.label: page 2
passages.text: One DSD People, Access and Culture | 2 Learning glossary continued Racism Ideas, conduct, and institutional arrangements that create or sustain racial disadvantage and advantage. It can involve individual behavior and patterns across policies or institutions; examining one does not make the other unimportant. Individual and systemic racial harm Individual harm concerns treatment in a particular interaction. Systemic analysis examines how repeated arrangements produce or sustain racial inequality. A concern about unfair treatment deserves consideration; a slogan about reverse racism should not replace examination of the facts or the appropriate complaint process. White privilege Advantages associated with being perceived as white in a society shaped by racial inequality. Recognizing those advantages does not mean every white person's life is easy or that effort and other barriers do not matter. Unconscious and implicit bias Overlapping terms for associations or judgments that may operate outside full awareness. Implicit measures study associations indirectly. Neither an informal exercise nor a course response diagnoses a person's beliefs. Affinity bias Favoring what or whom feels familiar or similar to oneself, without enough attention to the criteria that matter for the decision. Confirmation bias Giving more attention or weight to information that supports an existing belief while overlooking information that could challenge it.

passages.label: page 3
passages.text: One DSD People, Access and Culture | 3 Learning glossary continued Halo effect Allowing one favorable impression to influence a judgment about other qualities without checking the relevant evidence. Perception bias An interpretation influenced by prior expectations or stereotypes. Separating observation from interpretation can help a person examine that influence; it does not guarantee perfect objectivity. Intercultural competence The ability to understand different cultural perspectives and respond appropriately in context. Learning involves self-reflection, inquiry, practice, and feedback rather than memorizing rules about groups. Cultural humility An ongoing willingness to examine what one does not know, attend to power and context, and learn from people without expecting them to represent an entire group. Equity Examining barriers and differing circumstances so people have a fair opportunity to participate and benefit. It requires attention to how decisions work and whom they affect. Accessibility Designing information, environments, and participation so people with disabilities can use them. A general offer of help does not replace the relevant accessibility or accommodation arrangements.

passages.label: page 1
passages.text: One DSD People, Access and Culture | 1 Unconscious Bias in Everyday Decisions One DSD People, Access and Culture Foundation learning for all staff and supervisors A first impression can influence a decision before we notice the assumptions behind it. These activities help you distinguish what you observed from what you inferred, compare options consistently, and reconsider a familiar explanation. Unconscious and implicit bias are overlapping terms. This companion supports practice; it does not diagnose beliefs or require an Implicit Association Test. For all staff, including supervisors and managers. Participation is voluntary. You may use the practice cases, reflect privately, discuss an example, or pass. No one needs to disclose personal experiences, identities, or assessment results. What you will practice Separate the observation from the story Check familiar shortcuts Notice when an assumption becomes a routine Review the decision and repair the record Use with the full course https://one-dsd-people-access-culture-production.up.railway.app/courses/sf-unconscious-bias-everyday- decisions Participation and course completion in this program do not count toward DHS-required training credits unless management, a director, or DHS leadership expressly approves an exception.

passages.label: page 2
passages.text: One DSD People, Access and Culture | 2 1 Separate the observation from the story An observation describes what happened. An interpretation gives it meaning. 'A person spoke loudly' is different from 'the person was hostile.' Loudness may reflect frustration, a poor connection, hearing needs, a familiar speaking style, or something else. The point is to check the meaning relevant to the exchange, rather than choose a cultural explanation in advance. Automatic associations can influence attention and interpretation. That does not mean every quick judgment is wrong or that we can know someone's private beliefs from a single action. A useful pause makes room for evidence and another plausible account. Explore the example Practice example: During a phone conversation about a program notice, a staff member hears a raised voice and writes 'aggressive' in a draft note. The caller later explains that the connection was poor and they were trying to be heard. The original observation did not establish aggression. Try it Rewrite the note using only observable details relevant to the work. Add a neutral question, such as 'Can you hear me clearly, and what would you like me to explain about the notice?' Identify what new information would support or change your interpretation. Do not place a cultural or psychological label on the caller. Check your reasoning Which note stays closest to the evidence? A. The caller's culture makes them aggressive. B. The caller spoke loudly; the reason was not yet clear. C. The caller has an unconscious bias. Answer B. The second note describes an observation and its uncertainty. Neither a cultural explanation nor a diagnosis follows from speaking volume. Reflect if useful: Which words in my notes describe a person's actions, and which assign a motive?

passages.label: page 3
passages.text: One DSD People, Access and Culture | 3 2 Check familiar shortcuts Affinity bias can make familiarity feel like evidence of suitability. Confirmation bias can lead us to favor information that supports an existing view. A halo effect occurs when one favorable quality spills over into judgments about unrelated qualities. Perception can also be shaped by stereotypes that influence what we notice. These concepts help us examine a decision; they are not labels to assign to colleagues. Before comparing people or proposals, identify what the task actually requires. Ask the same core questions of each option. Look for information that could change your preferred explanation, and distinguish a relevant qualification from personal comfort. Explore the example Practice example: A reviewer favors a proposal from a familiar team because its previous presentation was polished. A less familiar team provides clearer evidence about the current question. Presentation skill may matter for some work, but it does not establish the quality of this analysis. Try it List three criteria relevant to the decision. Use them to compare both proposals. Identify which impression could be an affinity or halo effect, and what evidence would justify a different choice. Keep the judgment about the proposals rather than the character of either team. Check your reasoning What would best improve this comparison? A. Select the familiar team to avoid uncertainty. B. Select the unfamiliar team regardless of its evidence. C. Compare both proposals against the same relevant criteria and examine contrary evidence. Answer C. The third response tests the reasoning. Reversing a preference without examining the work simply replaces one shortcut with another. Reflect if useful: What evidence would make me reconsider a choice that already feels right?

passages.label: page 4
passages.text: One DSD People, Access and Culture | 4 3 Notice when an assumption becomes a routine A label can travel through a process. If a person is described as difficult, later staff may approach them defensively before reviewing the actual request. Repeated assumptions can influence whose concerns are heard and how much explanation they receive. Reviewing the routine helps us move beyond asking whether one individual meant well. A complaint history does not establish the merits of a new request or the person's character. Attend to the current question, relevant facts, and any actual safety requirements. Keep complaint handling and formal decisions within their appropriate processes. Explore the example Practice example: A staff member reviewing a service inquiry sees that the person previously challenged a decision. A colleague suggests avoiding contact because the person is 'always difficult.' The file does not describe a current safety concern. The staff member still needs to understand and respond to the inquiry. Try it Separate relevant information from a judgment about the person. Draft an opening that explains the purpose of contact and invites the person's current question. Identify where a formal complaint should be directed if that is what the person wants. The exercise does not ask you to resolve a real complaint. Check your reasoning How should the previous complaint affect this inquiry? A. Use relevant facts without assuming the current request lacks merit or that the person is unsafe. B. Treat it as proof that the person should receive less help. C. Promise the requested outcome to prevent another complaint. Answer A. The first response preserves a fair examination of the current inquiry. It neither penalizes the person for a complaint nor promises an outcome before review. Reflect if useful: Where could an unsupported label keep being repeated in a process I use?

passages.label: page 5
passages.text: One DSD People, Access and Culture | 5 4 Review the decision and repair the record Recognizing a shortcut is a beginning. A practical response might correct an inaccurate description, compare evidence more consistently, or make an opportunity clearer. If your action affected someone, acknowledge what happened without asking them to comfort you or accept an apology. Learning about bias does not establish that bias has disappeared. Research on changing implicit measures also does not justify treating a test score as a reliable verdict about a person's future conduct. Examine the decision and its effects, and make room for feedback that challenges your preferred account. Explore the example Practice example: A team discovers that 'did not engage' in its meeting notes meant a colleague did not speak immediately. The colleague had sent written comments that were overlooked. The team corrects the summary, considers the comments, and agrees to review both spoken and written contributions before recording a decision. Try it Draft a brief correction naming the inaccurate statement, the evidence that changes it, and the practical repair. Identify how the team could check whether written contributions are considered in later decisions. Use the practice case without collecting individual bias scores or personal histories. Check your reasoning Which statement is supported after this correction? A. Everyone on the team is now free from bias. B. The team corrected an unsupported description and changed how it considers input. C. Written comments are always more useful than spoken comments. Answer B. The second statement describes what the example establishes. It does not turn one correction into a claim about everyone's beliefs or all future decisions. Reflect if useful: What would help me correct an assumption promptly and without becoming defensive?

passages.label: page 1
passages.text: One DSD People, Access and Culture | 1 Understanding White Privilege One DSD People, Access and Culture Foundation learning for all staff and supervisors White privilege describes advantages associated with being perceived as white in a society where racial inequality shapes opportunities and treatment. It does not mean that every white person has an easy life or that effort is unimportant. These activities help you examine how an ordinary practice can make access easier for some people, and what a more equitable approach could involve. For all staff, including supervisors and managers. Participation is voluntary. You may use the practice cases, reflect privately, discuss an example, or pass. No one needs to disclose personal experiences, identities, or assessment results. What you will practice Recognize advantage without ranking hardship Look at how opportunity travels Keep discussion open without putting someone on display Turn understanding into a fairer opportunity Use with the full course https://one-dsd-people-access-culture-production.up.railway.app/courses/div-f01-white-privilege Participation and course completion in this program do not count toward DHS-required training credits unless management, a director, or DHS leadership expressly approves an exception.

passages.label: page 2
passages.text: One DSD People, Access and Culture | 2 1 Recognize advantage without ranking hardship A person can work hard and still benefit from a barrier they did not have to face. Race, income, disability, family responsibilities, and other circumstances affect experience in different ways. Recognizing one kind of advantage does not settle every question about a person's life. It gives us a more specific question: does this practice create an additional racial barrier, and what evidence would help us understand it? Consider both personal interactions and repeated arrangements. Who is assumed to belong? Whose expertise is recognized without extra proof? These are questions to investigate, not conclusions to attach to a person because of their identity. Explore the example Practice example: Two colleagues describe working their way through college. One also describes repeated doubts about whether they earned their place because of their race. A listener responds that everyone has struggled, so race cannot be relevant. Shared hardship is real, but it does not answer the specific concern about racial treatment. Try it Write a response that acknowledges both accounts without comparing whose life was harder. Then identify the specific treatment that needs examination. A useful response might begin: 'Both experiences matter. I also want to understand the additional barrier you described.' No colleague needs to supply a personal story for this activity. Check your reasoning What is the most useful next step in this example? A. Ask who had the harder life before considering the concern. B. Acknowledge both accounts and examine the particular racial barrier described. C. Assume racial advantage explains every difference between the colleagues. Answer B. The second response keeps the specific concern visible without ranking hardship or treating race as the only influence on a person's life. Reflect if useful: When do I use a shared experience to connect, and when might it keep me from hearing an important difference?

passages.label: page 3
passages.text: One DSD People, Access and Culture | 3 2 Look at how opportunity travels An opportunity can be formally open while reaching only a familiar circle. Invitations, informal sponsorship, and unwritten expectations affect who can take part. A repeated pattern can preserve an existing advantage even when no one explicitly announces an exclusion. Do not assume that a small example establishes a racial disparity. Ask what is known about access, who has not been heard, and whether the same practice repeats. When reliable evidence indicates a racial pattern, examine the process that may sustain it rather than reducing the explanation to a single person's intention. Explore the example Practice example: A policy team shares a development opportunity during an informal gathering. Several people who rarely attend hear about it after selections are made. The team knows the invitation was uneven. It does not yet know whether the pattern differs by race, work schedule, disability, or another circumstance. Try it Map how someone would hear about the opportunity, understand the criteria, and express interest. Identify one step that relies on an existing relationship. Draft a clearer invitation and a consistent selection approach. Identify what further information would be needed before claiming a racial pattern; do not collect colleagues' personal identity details for a learning exercise. Check your reasoning Which conclusion is supported by the information available? A. Access to the invitation was uneven; the team should examine the process and any supported patterns. B. The example proves the racial identity of everyone who benefited. C. An opportunity cannot be inequitable unless someone intended exclusion. Answer A. The first response separates a known access problem from an unverified explanation. Repeated processes deserve examination even when exclusion was not intended. Reflect if useful: Which opportunities in my work depend on knowing whom to ask?

passages.label: page 4
passages.text: One DSD People, Access and Culture | 4 3 Keep discussion open without putting someone on display Learning about racial advantage can bring questions, uncertainty, or discomfort. A useful discussion examines ideas and evidence while respecting each person's choice about what to share. It does not require a colleague of color to prove the subject through a personal experience or speak for an entire community. Listen to the concern before explaining your intention. If an action caused harm, a specific acknowledgment and a practical correction can be more useful than asking the affected person to reassure you. An educational discussion also should not decide the validity of an individual complaint; that belongs in the appropriate process. Explore the example Practice example: During a learning discussion, someone asks the only Black participant to tell a painful story so others will understand. The facilitator pauses the request and offers a prepared practice example instead. The participant remains free to contribute, stay quiet, or leave the discussion. Try it Write two sentences a facilitator could use. First, remove the expectation of disclosure. Second, return to the learning question. For example: 'No one needs to share a personal experience. Let's examine who can access the opportunity in our example and what might need to change.' Check your reasoning Which response supports both learning and the participant's choice? A. Ask again because a personal story will be more convincing. B. Stop all discussion of racial inequality. C. Use a prepared case and let each person decide whether to contribute. Answer C. The third response keeps the subject available while removing pressure on one person to educate the group through personal disclosure. Reflect if useful: What helps me stay curious when a discussion challenges how I understand fairness?

passages.label: page 5
passages.text: One DSD People, Access and Culture | 5 4 Turn understanding into a fairer opportunity A practical response begins with the process you can influence. You might explain selection criteria, make an invitation easier to find, examine whose ideas receive credit, or improve the way feedback reaches a decision. Ask affected people what would help without assuming that your preferred solution meets their needs. A change should be judged by what happens after it is used. More invitations may broaden awareness, but they do not by themselves establish that selection was fair. Review the relevant steps and remain open to changing an approach that leaves a barrier in place. Explore the example Practice example: A team replaces informal invitations with an open notice and explains how proposals will be considered. A staff member points out that the notice still uses unexplained terms. The team revises the notice and checks whether people outside its usual network can understand how to participate. Try it Choose one improvement in the practice process. Explain the barrier it addresses, the part still uncertain, and what feedback would help judge its usefulness. Use the application's Equity Analysis Toolkit when a broader policy or program decision needs examination. Do not promise a change outside your own responsibility. Check your reasoning What would help the team learn whether its change is useful? A. Check whether people can understand and use the invitation and examine how selection works. B. Count posted notices and declare the problem solved. C. Require everyone to report a personal privilege score. Answer A. The first response examines access and the decision process. A notice count or personal score cannot establish that the opportunity became fairer. Reflect if useful: What is one ordinary practice I can examine without making assumptions about another person's life?

passages.label: Overview
passages.text:
DSD Equity Implementation Work Plan
The Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant leads One DSD People, Access and Culture. This document supports planning and review; proposed assignments, measures, resources and schedules must be confirmed with the people responsible. It does not create new DHS policy or replace required decision authority.
Operationalizing equity across the Disability Services Division, aligned to the six ADSA Equity and Inclusion Implementation Plan goals
One DSD People, Access and Culture

passages.label: Purpose and how to read this plan
passages.text:
This plan turns the six ADSA Equity and Inclusion Implementation Plan goals into dated, owned work for the Disability Services Division (DSD) over 18 months, an agreed eighteen-month period. It is built on five source documents and on the One DSD People, Access and Culture program, which already supplies the toolkit, the DSD Equity Needs Assessment, and One DSD Consult.
Two facts shape every choice here. First, DHS is in an assessment phase: the Office of Strategy and Performance, the Office of Innovation and Impact, and the Office of Employee Culture finished interviews and analysis for the 2025–2026 Equity Outcome Map and are now in co-creation, so enterprise metrics and roles may still move. Second, DSD staff have already told us, through 71 interviews and the needs assessment, what they need. The plan therefore starts with what DSD controls, aligns to the Outcome Map metrics where they exist, and leaves clearly marked seams where enterprise decisions will plug in.
Read it top down. Sections 2 and 3 are the honest starting point. Section 4 is the operating model. Section 5 is the timeline. Sections 6 through 11 are the six goal workstreams, each with actions, owners, dates, and measures. Sections 12 through 14 cover measurement, risk, and the decisions leadership needs to make now.

passages.label: What the source materials tell us
passages.text:
The five inputs agree on the destination and differ on altitude. The enterprise materials define outcomes and metrics; the ADSA materials define six goals; the DSD materials are tools waiting for a structure to run them. This plan supplies that structure.
Source | What it is | What it gives this plan | Where it is silent
ADSA Equity Work (Deqa Sayid, Jan 2024) | Director's framing deck: One Minnesota, DHS Strategic Plan, DHS Equity Policy, equity dashboard design | The six policy objectives, the dashboard categories (Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, Access), the three leadership supports, and named gaps in retention, procurement, and CLAS | Division-level owners, dates, and how DSD feeds the dashboard
Equity Outcome Map 2025–2026 (OSP, OII, OEC) | Enterprise evaluation: 25+ documents, 34 interviews, theory of change, four desired outcomes, key activities, key metrics, 13 known barriers | The metrics DSD should report against and the barriers DSD must design around | Still in co-creation; no division assignments yet
Equity Review Intake Form and DSD DEIA Status Report Form | Two draft reporting instruments: a manager initiative submission and a leadership status report to the ADSA Equity Director | The reporting backbone, once the two forms are reconciled into one cadence | No schedule, no definition of done, no link to the toolkit's analysis records
Continuum on Becoming an Anti-Racist Multicultural Organization (Crossroads) | Six-stage developmental model from Exclusive to Fully Inclusive | A shared, honest yardstick for self-assessment and for naming what structural change means in practice | Not a measurement instrument; use it for dialogue and direction, not scoring
Three themes run through all five. Equity is treated as an add-on when roles are unclear and accountability is thin; the Outcome Map names both as barriers, and the Equity Team draft anticipates the same concern as tokenism. Learning only changes practice when it is tied to a decision, which is why the Equity Analysis Toolkit appears in Goals 1, 2, and 5 and in the enterprise metrics. And nothing survives leadership change unless it is written into structures, cadences, and job expectations, which the Continuum calls the shift from identity change to structural change.

passages.label: Where DSD sits today
passages.text:
DSD has more equity assets than most divisions and less structure to run them. Measured against the Crossroads Continuum, the division has moved past symbolic change and into identity change: it has a named equity role, a needs assessment built from 71 staff interviews, a working toolkit, a consult pathway, and leadership that commissioned all of it. What it does not yet have is the structural layer, the standing team, the decision points where analysis is required, the reporting rhythm, and the job expectations that make equity routine rather than relational.
This is a working judgment, not a score. The Continuum is a conversation tool, and the DSD Equity Team should revisit this placement with staff in its first quarter.
The Outcome Map's 13 known barriers map onto DSD as follows. Items marked "DSD controls" are addressed in this plan; items marked "enterprise" are tracked as dependencies in Section 13.
Known barrier (Outcome Map) | How it shows up in DSD | Who can move it
Unclear roles and responsibilities | No charter yet for an Equity Team; maintenance, support, accessibility, and records roles for the program still unnamed | DSD controls
Equity seen as add-on or optional | Toolkit use is voluntary; no decision type requires an analysis | DSD controls
Leadership and staff accountability | Intake and status forms drafted but no cadence, owner, or consequence attached | DSD controls
Consistent foundational knowledge | Needs assessment shows uneven understanding of what equity work is; six-goal learning standards exist in the program but are not yet assigned | DSD controls
Resources: staffing and time | One consultant role carries design, delivery, support, and reporting | DSD leadership decides
Silos | Equity work sits apart from program, contracting, and hiring workflows | DSD controls, with ADSA partners
Data access and decision making | DSD has no disaggregated workforce or service data feed of its own | Enterprise, with DSD request
Superficial community engagement | Advisory council and Tribal engagement happen at ADSA level; DSD has no feedback loop of its own | Shared
Retention and turnover | Dashboard measures exist on paper, not in a DSD report | Enterprise data, DSD reporting
Training and capacity | IDI, OAR, and TSRT exist; DSD completion rates unknown | Shared
Work culture; systemic racism; political climate and safety | Real, named by staff, and beyond any single plan; this plan creates safe structures and does not overclaim | Everyone, over time
The honest implication: the first two quarters of this plan are mostly about building structure, not announcing results. Results that are reported before the structure exists do not last.

passages.label: Operating model
passages.text:
Four structures carry the plan. Each has one accountable owner, a fixed cadence, and a written output, so the work continues when any one person is away.
Structure | Who | Cadence | Output | Accountable to
DSD Equity program review group | Division Director , Manager , Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant | Monthly, 45 minutes | Decisions log; review of status report | ADSA Equity and Inclusion Director
DSD Equity Team | 8 to 12 members: core members, contributors, and supporters per the interest form; lived experience of disability, race, and LGBTQIA+ identities required in core membership; at least two direct-service staff and one supervisor | Core: twice monthly, 60 minutes; full team: monthly | Meeting summaries published to staff; quarterly you-said-we-did report | program review group
Goal leads | One manager or supervisor per ADSA goal, named by the program review group, supported by the consultant | Quarterly check-in with the program review group; monthly with the consultant | Goal section of the DSD DEIA Status Report | program review group
One DSD program operations | Consultant, plus named maintenance, support, accessibility, and records contacts | Weekly triage of Consult requests; quarterly content review | Consult log; toolkit release notes; analysis records archive | program review group
Decision points where an equity analysis is required. Starting in Phase 1, four decision types are proposed for review before proceeding with a completed toolkit analysis attached: new or materially revised DSD policy or procedure; new or renewed contracts and grants above the threshold the program review group sets; hiring plans for supervisor and above; and any public-facing communication or service change affecting access. This is the single most important structural change in the plan. It is what moves equity from optional to routine.
Reporting backbone. The two draft forms become one instrument with two layers. Managers submit the Equity Review Intake Form for each initiative as it starts and as it closes. The consultant compiles those submissions, the Consult log, and the toolkit analysis records into the DSD DEIA Status Report, which the program review group reviews and sends to the ADSA Equity Director quarterly. Nothing is reported twice, and every reported item traces to a record.
Time commitment. Core Equity Team members: a proposed four hours a month, subject to agreement with the responsible supervisor. Goal leads: proposed time to be agreed. program review group: one hour a month plus quarterly report review. The consultant leads this program; capacity needs should be reviewed; Section 14 asks leadership to confirm that.

passages.label: Phased timeline
passages.text:
The plan runs in four phases over 18 months. Phase 0 secures decisions, names people, and listens to staff. Phase 1 builds the structures and trains before anything is required. Phase 2 runs the full cadence and reports real numbers. Phase 3 reassesses against the Continuum and realigns to whatever DHS co-creation has settled.
implementation timeline · 4 phases, 5 milestones, proposed timing to confirm to proposed timing to confirm
The dashed line marks the one date that changes practice: from proposed timing to confirm, the four decision types in Section 4 are proposed for review before proceeding with a toolkit analysis. Everything before it exists so that date works; everything after it reports on whether it did.
Phase gates. Phase 1 does not start until the six leadership decisions in Section 14 are recorded. Phase 2 does not start until the Equity Team charter is signed and every unit has completed a practice lab. Phase 3 starts on schedule regardless, because its purpose is to look honestly at what did and did not happen.

passages.text:

passages.label: Overview
passages.text:
One DSD data and metrics framework
The Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant leads One DSD People, Access and Culture. This document supports planning and review; proposed assignments, measures, resources and schedules must be confirmed with the people responsible. It does not create new DHS policy or replace required decision authority.
Data and metrics framework
Disability Services Division (DSD) · For DSD leaders, goal leads, named contacts, the One DSD Team and the Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant

passages.label: 1. What this framework does
passages.text:
This framework recommends what DSD should measure to know whether the One DSD People, Access and Culture program, and the division's equity work as a whole, is making a difference. It covers four things:
The program itself: all thirteen functions of the application, from Ask and the Library to guided practice, help requests and the One DSD Team.
The six ADSA equity goals: Eliminate Disparities, Community Engagement, Hiring and Retention, Learning and Development, Contracts and Procurement, and Communication and Accessibility.
The two areas the goals do not fully cover: leadership and accountability, and workplace culture and belonging. Both are pillars of the program's Equity Strategic Framework.
How to collect, protect, report and act on the numbers, and who owns each one.
It lines up with the DHS Equity Policy's six objectives, the four outcomes in the DHS-wide Equity Outcome Map, the Equity Strategic Framework's measurement approach.

passages.label: 2. Principles
passages.text:
Measure decisions and outcomes, not clicks. Use of the program matters only if it leads to better decisions and smaller gaps. Every function is measured three ways: was it offered (delivery), did people use it in their work (use), and did anything change (benefit). This follows the program's own evaluation rule of examining delivery, application and benefit separately.
Three kinds of signs over time. Signs the work is happening (early), signs how we work is changing (middle), and signs results are improving (later). Do not mistake activity for results.
Totals only for the program; break down by group where gaps live. The program never tracks, scores or profiles an individual, and it never asks users for demographic details. Gaps between groups are measured in DSD's workforce, service, contract and engagement data, where they actually occur, and are always broken down by race, ethnicity, Tribal affiliation, disability, language, age, gender, veteran status and region where the data allows.
The consultant leads program measurement. Contributors measure the work for which they are responsible. Each goal lead and named contact collects and reports their own numbers. Leaders decide what matters. The consultant leads the program and helps design measures and read results. Source owners remain responsible for the accuracy and appropriate use of their data.
Fewer, better numbers. A small set of headline numbers goes in the quarterly report. Everything else is kept for the annual review or for answering questions.
Every number has a purpose. For each measure we know who uses it, what decision it informs, and what we do if it moves the wrong way.
People's accounts count too. Numbers are paired with what staff, people who use services, families, communities and Tribal Nations tell us. A number without a story is incomplete.
Protect people. Follow the Minnesota Government Data Practices Act, hide small numbers that could identify someone, respect Tribal data sovereignty, and keep case, medical, personnel and complaint details out of the program.

passages.label: 7. The quarterly scorecard
passages.text:
The full set above is too much for one report. The quarterly report carries 21 headline numbers: six for program health, two for each ADSA goal, one for leadership and two for workplace culture. These are the numbers built into the One DSD Quarterly Report. The rest are reviewed yearly or when a question comes up.
Area | Headline numbers

passages.label: 8. Yearly measures
passages.text: Review these at the agreed review point: workforce representation compared with the communities DSD serves; promotions and moves into leadership by group; the full climate survey by group; community members' sense of being heard; contract dollars by organization type; the full set of service gaps; group-level intercultural development where assessed; and a program evaluation that looks at delivery, use and benefit for all thirteen functions.

passages.label: 9. Warning signs and what happens next
passages.text:
A warning sign means leaders look into it now, not at the next report. Leaders set the levels. Recommended starting points:
Warning sign | Suggested starting level | What happens
A priority service gap | Ratio of 1.3 or higher, or worse two quarters in a row | Goal 1 lead and program owner review causes and propose a fix within one quarter
A key decision without an equity review | Any | Leaders review the decision and whether it should be reopened
Significant decision with no input from burdened groups | Any | Goal 2 lead and decision owner plan input before the next step
A group leaving at a higher rate | Clearly higher than others two quarters in a row | Goal 3 lead and Human Resources look at stay and exit themes and propose action
Learning not applied | Confidence up, application flat two quarters | Goal 4 lead changes the learning design
Contract applicants dropping off | Higher drop-off for culturally specific, small, Tribal or Greater Minnesota organizations | Goal 5 lead reviews the process and support offered
Access barriers unresolved | At or above the number leaders set | Goal 6 lead and accessibility contact set a fix schedule
Belonging or trust drop | Agreed number of points, overall or for any group | One DSD Team and leaders hold listening sessions
A goal or area without an owner | Any | Leaders name an owner

passages.label: 10. Protecting people and the data
passages.text:
Totals only for the program. No user accounts tied to activity, no individual learning scores, no time-on-page tracking, no demographic questions to users.
Hide small numbers. Do not show any group with fewer people than the agreed minimum (often ten). Combine quarters or groups if needed.
Survey privacy. Anonymous; results shown only for groups large enough; limits explained before people answer.
Tribal data. Data about Tribal members and Tribal lead agencies is shared only with consent and under agreement, and Tribal Nations see results about them first.
Data practices. Follow the Minnesota Government Data Practices Act and HIPAA where service data is involved; keep data only as long as the records schedule allows.
No personnel records. The program and this framework do not hold, create or feed personnel records.
Who can see what. Leaders and goal leads see the full report. Staff see the Team page, "you said, we did" and the public summary. Raw data stays with its owner.

passages.label: 11. Data gaps to start on now
passages.text:
Service data broken down by race, language and lead agency, through the ADSA Equity Director (expect delays; use DSD-held data in the meantime).
Tribal affiliation in service data, which is often incomplete; work with Tribal lead agencies under agreement.
Deaf, hard-of-hearing and blind status in service data, which is usually not captured; estimate from assessment communication fields where allowed.
Applicant-flow data by group at division level, through Human Resources.
Contract applicant data by organization type, which may not be collected today; add it to solicitations.
Network settings that allow site totals by DSD unit without identifying individuals; ask MNIT.

passages.label: Overview
passages.text:
One DSD Quarterly Report
For each quarter, complete Evidence and sources with the source, reporting period, method, numerator and denominator where relevant, sample size and limits. This context appears in every report view and in saved report files. When an older file has no evidence entry, add it before interpreting or sharing the results.
The Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant leads One DSD People, Access and Culture. This document supports planning and review; proposed assignments, measures, resources and schedules must be confirmed with the people responsible. It does not create new DHS policy or replace required decision authority.
How to use it
Disability Services Division (DSD) · One DSD People, Access and Culture

passages.label: What it is
passages.text:
The consultant leads program reporting, drawing on updates from the people responsible for each goal and area of work. The Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant supports them by advising, coaching and connecting people, and helps put the report together. The Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant leads the program and coordinates reporting. Each contributor remains responsible for the work and information they provide.
The quarterly report is one file, One_DSD_Quarterly_Report_Dashboard.html. Double-click it and it opens in your web browser. You do not need the internet or a login. It automatically saves in this browser on this device. Download a report to keep a separate copy or share an approved summary. No report is sent to the program server.
The report starts empty so practice numbers cannot be mistaken for actual results. Choose View examples to explore a separate practice report, and Return to real report when ready. Examples cannot be relabeled as real or overwrite a real browser save. Enter verified aggregate numbers in the real report and leave unavailable values blank.

passages.label: The four pages
passages.text:
Use the buttons under the title to switch pages. These views do not enforce access permissions. Share only the reviewed view or summary appropriate for the audience; a full report file contains every view. Recover previous save can restore the previous browser copy after a mistaken change.
Page | Who it is for | What is on it
For leaders | DSD leaders and the ADSA Equity Director | How things are going overall, six key numbers, what went well, what could get in the way, decisions leaders need to make, warning signs, progress on the six ADSA equity goals, progress toward the end-of-year checkpoint, and what is coming next.
For the One DSD Team | The Team and all staff | How many members and which units (no names), Open Hours, decisions the Team reviewed and what changed, "you said, we did", what staff are saying overall, and what the Team asks leaders to do.
Owners and support | Goal leads, named contacts and the Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant | Who owns each goal and area and whether they have time, keeping the program running, requests for help, numbers, the coaching and support the consultant gave, risks, support planned for next quarter, the checkpoint, and every number side by side with last quarter.
All numbers over time | Everyone | A chart for each number, quarter by quarter.

passages.label: Every quarter, step by step
passages.text:
Open the report file. Click Open saved report and choose last quarter's saved file (one-dsd-quarterly-report.json).
Click Add a quarter. A form opens with the quarter's name already filled in.
Each person fills in their own part. Each goal lead fills in their goal's status, this quarter and next quarter. The upkeep, support and data contacts fill in their sections and their numbers. Leaders fill in the summary, the owners section and the checkpoint items that are done. The consultant fills in the coaching and support given and the support planned. If a number is not available yet, leave it blank. It will show as a dash, not a zero.
The One DSD Team fills in its own section.
The consultant leads preparation of the report with input from the people responsible for each area. Contributors check the accuracy of their own information.
Click Done, then Save report. The file goes to your Downloads folder. Move it to the team's shared folder.
Click Print this view to print the selected page, or choose Save as PDF in the print window. Review the audience and content before sharing each view.
Send the report to DSD leaders. Leaders read the "For leaders" page, make the decisions listed, and sign off.
Share the Team page and the "you said, we did" summary with all staff. Send the leaders' page to the ADSA Equity Director with the DSD status report.
To look at an earlier quarter, choose it from the list at the top. To fix something, choose the quarter and click Add or change this quarter's numbers.

passages.label: Warning signs
passages.text:
The report checks for warning signs every quarter. If one appears, it shows in red on the leaders' page with who should act. A warning means leaders should look into it now, not wait for the next report.
Warning sign | Who acts
A goal or area of work has no named owner, so work may drift to the consultant | Leaders name an owner
A key decision went ahead without an equity review | Leaders decide whether to reopen it
The top priority service gap reaches the warning level, or grows two quarters in a row | Goal 1 lead and the program owner
Community input before decisions goes down two quarters in a row | Goal 2 lead with decision owners
The gap between groups in who stays stays at or above the warning level two quarters in a row | Goal 3 lead and Human Resources
Fewer people use what they learned, two quarters in a row | Goal 4 lead
A larger contract or grant went out without an equity review | Goal 5 lead
Accessible materials or on-time interpreters go down two quarters in a row | Goal 6 lead
The belonging and trust score drops, or the gap between groups reaches the warning level | One DSD Team and leaders
The starting warning levels support discussion; they are not policy requirements. Review thresholds with the consultant and appropriate data owners before using them to interpret results. Changing a threshold affects this report file. Retain an earlier export when documenting a change.

passages.label: The numbers
passages.text:
The report carries the 21 headline numbers from the One DSD Data and Metrics Framework:
Program health (6): units using the program; people who used something in their work; decisions changed by a review; help requests finished; time to first reply; pages current and accessible.
Each of the six ADSA goals (2 each): shown beside each goal on the leaders' page.
Leadership (1): goals and areas with a named owner.
Workplace culture (2): belonging and trust score, and the gap between groups.
All of them are totals for the division. Some numbers, like the gap between groups in who stays, come from more detailed tables; put the one summary number here and keep the detailed table with the written report. The full set of measures is in the framework and is reviewed once a year. If a number is not available yet, leave it blank. In Year 1 many numbers will be blank; that is expected.

passages.label: Privacy
passages.text: Never put names, case details, personnel details or any one person's results in the report. Describe people by role, unit or community. The program keeps no personnel records, and this report must not become one.
